In this work, we introduce a sequential-dispatch measurement method and show that naive single-operation measurements overestimate per-dispatch cost by conflating dispatch with synchronization. Using our method, we measure the per-dispatch cost and show that it is independent of data type used. Through a controlled fusion experiment, we show that the dispatch overhead, not kernel quality, is the bottleneck at batch size 1, and isolate the dispatch count as the cause. We conclude that at batch size 1, the effective approach to LLM inference optimization in WebGPU is reducing dispatch count. Our findings point to dispatch amortization, in the inference engines and in the WebGPU specification, as a path to practical browser-based inference.
comment: Accepted to COLM 2026 Workshop on Methods and Opportunities at Small Scale (MOSS) and COLM 2026 The 2nd Workshop on Efficient Reasoning
♻ ☆ Characterizing WebGPU Dispatch Overhead for LLM Inference Across Four GPU Vendors, Three Backends, and Three Browsers
Jędrzej Maczan
WebGPU's security-focused design imposes per-operation validation that compounds across the many small dispatches in neural network inference, yet the true cost of this overhead is poorly characterized. We present a systematic characterization of WebGPU dispatch overhead for LLM inference at batch size 1, spanning four GPU vendors (NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, Intel), two native implementations (Dawn, wgpu-native) and three browsers (Chrome, Safari, Firefox), and two model sizes (Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B). Our primary contribution is a sequential-dispatch methodology that reveals naive single-operation benchmarks overestimate dispatch cost by ${\sim}20\times$. The true per-dispatch cost of WebGPU API overhead alone is 24-36 $μ$s on Vulkan and 32-71 $μ$s on Metal, while the total per-operation overhead including Python cost is ${\sim}95$~$μ$s, which turns out to be a distinction critical for optimization. On Vulkan, kernel fusion improves throughput by 53%, while CUDA fusion provides no benefit, confirming that per-operation overhead is a primary differentiator. LLM inference was tested across three major operating systems (Linux, Windows, macOS). We built $\texttt{torch-webgpu}$, a PrivateUse1-based out-of-tree PyTorch backend and an FX-to-WebGPU compiler, which on our reference platform achieves 11--12% of CUDA performance. At dtype-matched float32, RTX PRO 2000 achieves 1.4$\times$ WebGPU's throughput despite ${\sim}6\times$ less compute than RTX 5090. For dispatch overhead, backend choice is the dominant factor, although implementation choice also matters substantially within a backend (2.2$\times$ for Metal). In terms of dispatch vs kernel compute efficiency, we conclude that at batch=1 with the current dispatch-heavy pipeline, per-operation overhead dominates regardless of kernel quality. All code, benchmarks, and raw data are open source.
comment: Superseded by arXiv:2608.08730. Please cite that version
♻ ☆ rush: Scalable Asynchronous Distributed Computing via Shared State in R
Marc Becker, Bernd Bischl
Many algorithms in statistics and machine learning can be parallelized in an asynchronous manner where workers need to communicate through shared state rather than execute independent tasks dispatched by a central controller. Especially in modern hyperparameter optimization and parallel black-box optimization with expensive objectives, this decentralized approach has become widespread, and several Python frameworks adopt it (e.g., Optuna, DeepHyper, and Hyperopt). However, all popular R packages for parallel computing follow a centralized controller-worker architecture that does not support this pattern. We present rush, an R package that provides a shared-state coordination layer for asynchronously parallelized iterative algorithms. rush uses a Redis database as a shared key-value store: workers read and write task data through the database and independently execute their own loops. The package provides a high-level API for managing tasks and their lifecycle, featuring sub-millisecond per-task overhead, robust error handling with automatic detection of lost workers, and efficient caching. rush optionally integrates with the mlr3 ecosystem, powering asynchronous optimization in the bbotk and mlr3tuning packages. We demonstrate the practical utility of rush by implementing asynchronous decentralized Bayesian optimization (ADBO) and benchmarking it on hyperparameter optimization of LightGBM across four datasets using 448 workers.
♻ ☆ HARTS: A Prefix-Sharing Training System for Agentic RL with Hybrid-Attention Models
Boyuan Meng, Peihua Bao, Hong Liu, Xiaowei Zhu, Chao Wang, Gen Li, Zhenxuan Pan
Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) generates irregular rollout trees, but trajectory-by-trajectory training recomputes their shared interaction histories. Existing training-time prefix-reuse systems do not jointly address state recovery, dense execution, and distributed training for hybrid-attention models. We present HARTS (Hybrid-Attention RL over Tree Structures), to our knowledge the first system to demonstrate training acceleration from arbitrary rollout-tree prefix sharing on real hybrid-attention models. A two-level planner constructs compression-oriented microbatches, then jointly refines their membership, cross-microbatch sharing, placement, and execution order. Within each sharing window, gradients from dependent microbatches accumulate before one backward pass through the shared prefix computation. Differentiable boundary-state handoff and bounded replay preserve the per-trajectory chunkwise numerical path, while a linear-time planner attains the global minimum number of sequential linear-attention calls under our packed chunkwise-call model. The runtime uses a common compact layout across attention and dense or mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, with support for distributed parallelism and activation recomputation. Recovering log-probabilities for each original trajectory position preserves RL objectives; for deterministic top-k routing without token dropping, occurrence counts restore MoE objective weights and expert-load statistics. On SWE-bench, HARTS delivers 4.77-10.45x the update throughput of trajectory-expanded training across two sampling schemes on 7.9B- and 124B-parameter hybrid-attention MoE models using 8-64 GPUs. On the 7.9B model, full-model logit differences are comparable to baseline self-rerun variation. The 124B model shows stable online learning trends through step 150 on SWE-bench and $τ^3$-Bench.
♻ ☆ Democratizing LLM Training with the Edge: Challenges, Systems, and the Road Ahead
Ziyue Luo, Jiaxuan Cai, Cedric LeDenmat, Srijith Nair, Fatemeh Nourzad, Rohith Krishnan, Qinhang Wu, Jifan Zhang, Sungjae Lee, Zhe Li, Peiwen Qiu, Siddharth Shah, Rishabh Sharma, Sundararajan Srinivasan, Yinglun Xia, Xue Zheng, Zidong Liu, Bicheng Ying, Kaushik Chowdhury, Gauri Joshi, Yingbin Liang, Robert Nowak, Srinivasan Parthasarathy, Saurav Prakash, Balaraman Ravindran, Sanjay Shakkottai, Ness B. Shroff, Haibo Yang, Aylin Yener, Jia Liu
The growing computational power of modern GPU data centers has let a few industrial giants train and deploy large language models (LLMs) on massive amounts of data. Yet the sheer scale of these models and their training data makes centralized development increasingly hard to sustain, and at the same time shuts out smaller institutions that hold relevant private data but lack comparable infrastructure. In this paper, we organize our positions on distributed LLM training around the pretraining and fine-tuning paradigms, covering federated learning, split learning, and decentralized approaches, and we assess their readiness for geo-distributed settings with heterogeneous hardware and unreliable connectivity. We then present a {\em unified} system architecture built around a cloud-hosted parameter server that coordinates heterogeneous clients over outbound gRPC connections, reusing one communication, compression, and fault-tolerance stack for both pretraining and a family of fine-tuning methods. We validate the design with real geo-distributed experiments on GPT-2 Medium and Llama3-1B pretraining across multiple university sites, showing stable convergence under realistic conditions. Finally, we chart the road ahead, identifying open problems that span frontier model support, elastic fault tolerance, adaptive compression, federated alignment, privacy and trust, incentive design, and system--algorithm co-design, all of which must be addressed to make democratized LLM training a reality.
♻ ☆ ActECC: Action Chunk Temporal Harnessing for Edge-Cloud Collaborative VLA Inference System
Zihao Zheng, Zhihao Mao, Hui Huang, Sicheng Tian, Hangyu Cao, Ziyun Zhang, Chenyue Li, Jiayu Chen, Maoliang Li, Hailong Zou, Guojie Luo, Xiang Chen
VLA models have emerged as the mainstream for embodied intelligence, which decouples reasoning and execution via action chunks. To enable real-time deployment of VLA models, existing studies investigate edge-cloud collaborative inference, which pose two challenges to the action chunk mechanism. (1) Edge-cloud collaboration complicates system latency components, hindering the determination of valid ranges for action chunks. (2) Latency fluctuations in cross-edge update links under edge-cloud scenarios make it difficult to schedule replanning requests. To address these, we analyze the key factors affecting action chunk usable ranges and replanning request timing, revealing phase dependence and edge-cloud latency constraints. Based on these insights, we propose ActECC, which enables Action Chunk Temporal Harnessing through kinematics-guided usable range assessment and delay-aware replanning scheduling. Experiments show that ActECC reduces per-action latency by up to 27.4% and cloud calls by up to 45.1%, while lowering average execution error compared with existing edge-cloud collaborative.
♻ ☆ KubePACS: Kubernetes Cluster Using Performant, Highly Available, and Cost Efficient Spot Instances
Taeyoon Kim, Kyumin Kim, Enrique Molina-Giménez, Pedro García-López, Kyungyong Lee
Cloud users aim to minimize cost while maximizing performance by selecting the most suitable instance types for their workloads. To reduce expenses, spot instances have been widely adopted due to their steep discounts compared to on-demand pricing. However, their use introduces reliability risks due to potential interruptions, and existing research has primarily focused on mitigating this trade-off from a cost or availability perspective alone. Despite the diversity in hardware capabilities among instance types, current provisioning systems tend to ignore performance variation, selecting nodes solely based on minimum resource requirements. In this paper, we present KubePACS, a Kubernetes-native spot instance provisioning system that constructs node pools optimized for both cost and performance while guaranteeing high availability. KubePACS formulates the node selection process as a multi-objective optimization problem, incorporating real-time data such as spot prices, performance benchmarks, and availability scores, including the multi-node Spot Placement Score (SPS). It solves this problem efficiently using an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) approach guided by the Golden Section Search (GSS) algorithm to find the optimal configuration. By integrating with the Karpenter node autoscaler, KubePACS jointly optimizes instance-type selection and node scaling decisions within a standard provisioning workflow. KubePACS also adopts a novel heuristic to support workload-specific preferences by scaling performance metrics for specialized instances. Through extensive evaluation across synthetic and real-world workloads, KubePACS demonstrates on average 55.09% and up to 81.06% higher performance per dollar over state-of-the-art solutions such as Karpenter, SpotVerse, and SpotKube, which only reference the spot instance prices and limited availability data.
comment: Accepted to the 27th ACM International Middleware Conference (Middleware 2026)
♻ ☆ OpenAgenet / OAN Yellow Paper: Technical Architecture for Trust-Governed Resource Identity and Discovery
Jinliang Xu
This yellow paper specifies the technical architecture and verification semantics of OpenAgenet (OAN), a protocol-neutral trust layer for heterogeneous Agent resources. The design combines did:oan decentralized identifiers (DIDs), verifiable credentials (VCs), on-chain infrastructure governance, and Root-verified resource packages. It defines the objects and lifecycle transitions that connect subject-control verification, Registrar admission, Root acceptance, authorized Discovery, and signed invocation. Infrastructure authorization requires both active governance state and a valid Root-issued credential; resource discovery additionally requires package integrity, current-version state, and authorized-domain coverage. Local OAN Identity signing material remains separate from public protocol objects. Integration profiles carry resource identity into the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol through Skill, Runtime, Sidecar, and Gateway interfaces without redefining native task semantics. The paper distinguishes protocol requirements from implementation choices and sets out security properties, persistence and recovery expectations, and conformance criteria. Together, these rules provide a technical basis for independently implemented registration, discovery, and identity-protected interaction within an OAN trust domain.

☆ Failure-Resilient and Verifiable Distributed Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Retrieval
Abdullah Al-Mamun
Distributed vector databases increasingly support security-sensitive applications, yet existing systems primarily protect index integrity or replica availability rather than the trustworthiness of retrieved results. Consequently, a compromised replica can return a plausible but manipulated result that remains cryptographically valid, while conventional replication and Byzantine defenses do not directly establish whether the retrieved results are trustworthy. We present TrustANN, a middleware layer that provides query-level trust for distributed approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) retrieval without modifying the underlying ANN algorithm. TrustANN introduces three complementary protocols: TrustBind, which verifies retrieval trust from authenticated, consistent, and failure-domain-independent replica evidence; CoordShift, which asynchronously constructs reusable coordination epochs outside the query critical path; and AvailGuard, which performs bounded recovery when replicas are unavailable, stale, or conflicting while preserving the trust criterion. Queries are marked Trusted only when sufficient independent evidence exists for every relevant shard; otherwise, TrustANN returns Unverified. On an AWS deployment using distributed FAISS HNSW, TrustANN reduces retrieval attack success rate from 1.000 to 0.000 under the tested Byzantine-retrieval attack with two-of-three replica verification. The verification layer increases clean p95 latency by only 9.36%. Under replica crashes, TrustANN maintains trusted retrieval through 33% failures and correctly returns Unverified when sufficient evidence is unavailable.
☆ Cross-Modal Data Co-Locality for Heterogeneous Storage Systems
Abdullah Al-Mamun
Distributed vector stores increasingly serve multimodal workloads whose representations are jointly accessed but independently partitioned and placed. As a result, cross-modal physical locality remains largely unoptimized. Multimodal queries can incur remote accesses and cross-tier data movement even when each modality's ANN search remains efficient. We present Coloc, a storage-management layer that makes cross-modal access locality a first-class data-layout signal. A Cross-Modal Access Graph combines semantic affinity, co-access, and temporal behavior. A movement-aware optimizer places frequently co-accessed vectors under capacity and topology constraints. A migration manager adapts placement as workloads shift by weighing locality gains against migration cost. A confidence-gated prefetcher hides remaining slow-tier latency. Coloc operates above existing ANN indexes without modifying embeddings, search, or retrieval semantics. We deploy Coloc on a multi-tier AWS testbed spanning GPU, NUMA-DRAM, NVMe, and S3. Coloc substantially reduces data movement and query latency while leaving ANN retrieval unchanged. Under a scheduled workload shift, its migration manager matches the locality of periodic global reorganization while moving 5.9x less data and completing 3.9x faster.
☆ NovaFabric: A Black-Box Recorder for AI Agents with Sealed, Replayable, Diffable and Auditable Runs
Mohsen Seyedkazemi Ardebili
An AI agent run is no longer a function call. It is a cascade of prompts, model calls, tool invocations, file and network effects and sub-agents. When such a run misbehaves, or an auditor asks what happened, logs and traces answer poorly: they are mutable, partial and cannot be re-executed. This technical report describes NovaFabric, an open-source (Apache-2.0) black-box recorder for AI agents that turns a run into a sealed, replayable, diffable and auditable evidence capsule. The design rests on two formats only. The Run Capsule is a directory of flat files and the source of truth; every database is a rebuildable index over capsules. The Evidence Bundle is the signed export for an auditor. Everything else follows existing standards: OpenTelemetry GenAI, OpenLineage, W3C PROV, in-toto/DSSE, RFC 3161 and CycloneDX. A single-node run is the smallest case of a distributed one; the schema supports a capsule hierarchy for Slurm arrays and Kubernetes jobs, though automatic parent finalization is library-only today. The report covers the architecture and the engines behind the verb chain capture, seal, replay, diff and audit: fail-closed mocked replay; a diff gate with a stable exit-code contract; DSSE signatures that bind their intent and a capsule root that commits to file names; a capsule treated as untrusted input; signer identity-trust levels with offline TSA and CRL checking; maker-checker promotion against an operator-held trust list; and a deny-by-default authorization table for every dashboard route. It presents no new experiments; the evaluation is in arXiv:2609.12582. Every count except the private ADR tally is generated by a probe script run on the public source at the v0.107.0 tag (150 top-level commands, 84 Python subpackages, 16,721 test functions), every capability carries an explicit maturity label, and honest-limits boxes state where the system stops.
comment: Technical report (Technical Overview, Second Edition). 75 pages, 16 figures. Describes NovaFabric v0.107.0. Companion to arXiv:2609.12582. Code: https://github.com/MSKazemi/novafabric
☆ Supervision Without Blocking: An Evidence-Driven Redesign of OTP-Style Fault Tolerance for Cooperative Runtimes
Sam Uwejan, Erdogan Dogdu
Actor frameworks on mainstream runtimes advertise Erlang/OTP-style supervision, but OTP's consistency contracts assume a synchronous, single-threaded supervisor, and ports inherit that assumption's absence as unexamined risk. We evaluated every supervision guarantee against pinned OTP documentation and source read verbatim, against the source of three further Rust actor frameworks at fixed revisions, and against the actor-model literature, recording the evidence behind each design decision. Blind adversarial audits and the cross-framework study surfaced 24 defect classes, of which eight reduce to one root cause: reconstructing, by explicit mechanism, the atomicity a synchronous supervisor gets implicitly. We introduce a supervision runtime that closes all 24 cataloged classes through supervisor-owned completion values, per-incarnation identity, and a single lifecycle state machine, validated by 241 tests including reverted-fix reproductions. The result holds OTP's verbatim-verified contracts while adding two properties OTP does not offer: a supervisor that remains responsive throughout group restarts, and message handlers that are never cancelled mid-execution. We delimit the forcing guarantees no cooperative runtime can honor.
☆ Speculative Decoding for Mixture-of-Experts Models: Expert Bytes, Kernel Bandwidth and the Best Draft Length
Yuzheng Lan
Speculative decoding checks several drafted tokens in one verification pass. On a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, consecutive tokens often select the same experts. A deduplicating engine reads each selected expert once per pass, so it requests fewer bytes than a per-slot engine, which reads it once per token. We write a step's time as the bytes each kernel requests over its effective bandwidth, plus fixed time. Under geometric acceptance, we derive from this step time when speculation is faster than plain decoding. The best draft length is a monotone staircase in the acceptance rate. We bound how a bandwidth error moves each result, and we check the main steps in Lean. Deduplication is faster exactly where its share $\bar u(n)$ of the per-slot bytes is below its ratio $r(n)$ of the per-slot bandwidth. On llama.cpp Metal, MLX-LM and llama.cpp CUDA, which we modified to deduplicate, the per-slot kernel has the higher effective bandwidth (r = 0.32 to 0.75). Thus deduplication is faster only from 5 to 8 tokens per pass, or never. We fit the bandwidths on one layer's expert operation, run alone, in under an hour per model. Bytes from routing traces over these bandwidths predict the time that deduplication saves. The measured saving lies inside its error bound at every point on CUDA and MLX-LM and at 36 of 48 points on Metal. The crossover is the first pass size at which deduplication is faster. The prediction places it within one pass size in 10 of 12 configurations of engine, model and depth. We computed these predictions after the measurements. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, operation times measured before its speculative runs give the best draft length on CUDA within one at all 22 acceptance values.
comment: 35 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables
☆ Prefix Keys and Values Matter Late: RIPE Caching for Self-Speculative Decoding in Looped Language Models
Dezhen Lu, Runguo Li, Zixiang Ni
A looped language model runs one block of layers $R$ times per token, so its key-value (KV) cache holds $R$ planes per recurrent layer, and self-speculative decoding (draft with a few loops, verify with all $R$) reads them all. We find that prefix keys and values matter late: at equal perturbation size, loops 25-32 are $e^{15.0}$ (Huginn-0125) and $e^{12.8}$ (Raven-Llama) times more sensitive than loops 2-9, and the planes approach the last one geometrically, at 0.88 and 0.81 per loop. Whether the deepest plane alone suffices then depends on how ripe the late planes are: on Raven, storing only it is indistinguishable from a bf16-to-fp32 change; on Huginn, 1% of positions carry 74% of its error. We turn this into RIPE, which stores the deepest plane everywhere except a window of recent positions kept at full depth. On Huginn, a 64-position window removes 89% of the tail positions at 11.9% of the full cache's memory (1024-token context), and any window at least as long as the draft block makes batched verification block-independent by construction. Nine pre-registered GPU batches back these results. Simple models of acceptance, decoding cost and memory, two of them checked on held-out measurements, account for the measured self-speculative speed-ups ($2.09\times$ with the full cache, $2.58\times$ with the deepest plane) and decompose the $2.24\times$ fixed-memory throughput gain of one shared plane.
☆ ScaleRLT: Exact Log-Probabilities and Fast Deferred Rollouts for Reinforcement Learning on Looped Transformers
Dezhen Lu, Zixiang Ni, Runguo Li
Looped language models such as Ouro reuse one block of layers several times per token. A rollout engine can batch the deeper loops of several response positions and run them only when a deep readout is due. This deferred schedule is fast, but the learner of an on-policy RL algorithm recomputes the sampled tokens' log-probabilities with a dense pass, and the two computations differ in floating point: in FP32 at 4096 tokens about 18% of the sampled tokens miss a $10^{-5}$ same-weight gate, and with bf16 weights nearly every token does. We use a hybrid learner log-probability, $\ell=\ell_{\mathrm{dense}}+\mathrm{sg}(\ell_{\mathrm{sched}}-\ell_{\mathrm{dense}})$, where $\mathrm{sg}$ denotes stop-gradient. Its value is a no-grad replay through the rollout's own schedule, and its gradient is the dense learner's. The replay reproduces the rollout bit for bit in all 167 FP32 and 28 bf16 real-weight cells we ran on three platforms, including rollouts whose batch shrinks at stop tokens, and the gradient has the same FP32 error as other dense implementations in all 102 pre-registered comparisons from 96 to 4096 tokens; the full GRPO loss of a training step matches a float64 reference to $3.1\times10^{-4}$. On one GPU, deferral raises rollout throughput by $1.47$ to $1.56\times$, and by $1.18$ to $1.54\times$ once every step runs from CUDA graphs, bit for bit. In a two-node GRPO loop, one-wave KV admission and CUDA graphs shorten an update by $2.71\times$ with the gate bitwise at every update, and four nodes keep the update time within 2% at the same per-GPU load. In 100-update runs held-out GSM8K accuracy rose from 23% to 82% with the mixed-depth readout that deferral relies on and from 34% to 90% with the native readout, which reached a higher accuracy in less time. For looped models beyond one node we analyse a ring mapping of layers to GPUs and measure its communication paths.
☆ From GPU to TPU with Coding Agents: What Works, What Fails, and What It Costs? ICSE 2027
Hui Sun, Anderson Uchôa, Wesley K. G. Assunção
A coding agent can migrate a machine learning workload, report success, and still change how the model trains. Rising compute costs, limited accelerator capacity, and vendor dependence are pushing organizations toward alternatives to graphics processing units (GPUs); a key question is whether agent-generated migrations to tensor processing units (TPUs) can be trusted and at what cost. We build a dataset of 148 PyTorch ML research projects and use Claude Code to migrate ten of them from NVIDIA GPUs to Google Cloud TPUs. We independently assess whether each migration runs, preserves numerical behavior, executes on the intended hardware, maintains the project's goal, and delivers acceptable performance. We also examine failures, human effort, and costs. Eight projects meet our project-goal criterion, and migrations require 2.4 human interventions on average. Of 70 execution attempts, 53 fail (76%), and 26 of these failures (49%) raise no error. The most frequent cause is repeated compilation and other execution inefficiencies, while interactions with third-party libraries can silently change the computation: in one four-chip migration, the agent reports success despite a change in gradient clipping that reduces accuracy from 86.53% to 84.89%. Execution costs vary widely: in one workload, TorchTPU, a PyTorch execution backend for TPUs, trains 1.86 times faster and 25% cheaper per run than the GPU. For practitioners, these findings motivate independent reference runs, verification under the intended hardware configuration, and workload-specific acceptance and stopping criteria that account for both computational and human costs.

☆ MANTA: Unlocking DAG Flexibility in Asynchronous BFT
Mohan Yu, Chenlin Wu, Jianyu Niu, Cong Wang, Chenyuan Wu
DAG-based BFT protocols marked a shift in consensus design by replacing single-leader proposal paths with concurrent block proposals linked through a shared graph, where references encode consensus evidence. However, under heterogeneous wide-area networks (WANs), existing designs suffer from prolonged rounds and degraded performance due to straggler effects. The root cause is rigid round advancement: replicas move in synchronized rounds, waiting for enough references from the previous round before advancing. We propose a flexible DAG growth framework for asynchronous BFT consensus. Our key observation is that while reference quorums are necessary for safety and liveness, they need not block every round advancement. Instead, the connectivity required for commitment can be accumulated across rounds. Within the framework, we instantiate MANTA, which combines flexible DAG growth to advance by relaxing round synchronization and flexible coin to trigger leader election and finality earlier. Experiments on heterogeneous WAN deployments show that MANTA reduces latency by approximately 30%-70% in our evaluation.
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, Proceedings of the 24th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation 2027
☆ Do Bio-Inspired Algorithms Save Energy in Data Centres? Separating Server Packing from Migration Search in Virtual Machine Consolidation
Yichiet Aun, Yu Hang Woo
Energy-efficient virtual machine (VM) consolidation matters as data centre electricity demand rises. Bio-inspired metaheuristics, including ant colony optimisation (ACO), particle swarm optimisation (PSO), and genetic algorithms, have reported substantial energy savings. However, these improvements are commonly evaluated against conventional allocation policies that differ in both initial VM placement and subsequent migration optimisation, making it difficult to determine the contribution of metaheuristic search. This study reproduces an existing consolidation implementation in CloudSim Plus and introduces a matched control that retains the same initial packing and empty-host deactivation mechanisms but excludes migration search. ACO, PSO, and a modified genetic algorithm (MGA) are evaluated across two fleet configurations and four workload regimes, with ten stochastic replications per condition. The matched control achieves energy savings of 0.8-81.4% relative to the spreading baseline, the amount available falling sharply as load rises, without migrations or incomplete workload execution. Across 24 comparisons, metaheuristic search increases energy consumption in 11 cases, produces identical outcomes in seven, and reduces consumption in six. Of these, ten increases and five reductions remain statistically significant after Holm correction. Five of the six apparent reductions coincide with unfinished tasks and disappear after normalisation by delivered computational work. Only ACO under light heterogeneous load retains a 3.22-percentage-point improvement (95% CI 2.96-3.47). These findings demonstrate that initial packing and host deactivation account for most of the measured energy savings in the examined implementations, highlighting the importance of matched control conditions and workload-completion measures for reliable evaluation of VM consolidation algorithms.

☆ InferScale: Kubernetes-Native Predictive Autoscaling for SLO-Aware AI Inference
Wen Huang
Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) is widely used for inference services, but reactive scaling is often too slow when pods take tens of seconds to become ready. The problem gets worse in shared clusters, where independent HPAs compete for the same resource budget and can hurt different tenants from run to run. We present InferScale, a Kubernetes-native autoscaler that combines inference-aware signals, short-horizon demand prediction, SLO-state control, fast-path spike handling, and tenant-priority headroom without replacing the default scheduler. We evaluate InferScale on Azure Kubernetes Service in two settings. On a real ResNet-50 ONNX workload with 21-second cold start, repeated ramp-burst runs improve SLO compliance from 47.8% +/- 1.5% under a stronger external-metric HPA to 65.3% +/- 9.0% under InferScale. In repeated controlled multi-tenant contention experiments, InferScale cuts Gold-tier SLO standard deviation from 16.1 to 1.2 percentage points and makes contention outcomes follow the priority policy more closely. Repeated single-service ablations show 6-8 percentage point degradation, with an exploratory priority ablation showing a 27-point drop under contention. The main takeaway is that, in startup-sensitive inference serving, the practical value of prediction lies less in precise forecasting than in moving the controller early enough to offset cold-start delay.
comment: 8 pages. Published in IEEE CLOUD 2026
☆ SGL: Towards a Bridging Model for Heterogeneous Hierarchical Platforms
Chong Li, Gaétan Hains
This paper introduces the Scatter-Gather parallel-programming and parallel-execution model in the form of a simple imperative Scatter-Gather Language (SGL). Its design is based on past experience with bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) programming and BSP language design. SGL's novel features are motivated by the last decade's move towards multi-level and heterogeneous parallel architectures involving multi-core processors, graphics accelerators and hierarchical routing networks in the largest multiprocessing systems. The design of SGL is coherent with L. Valiant's Multi-BSP while offering a programming interface that is even simpler than the primitives of Bulk-Synchronous Parallel ML (BSML). SGL appears to cover a large subset of all BSP algorithms while avoiding complex message-passing programming. Like all BSP-inspired systems, it supports predictable, portable and scalable performance. Moreover, SGL's explicit data distribution will allow automatic or programmable load-balancing.
♻ ☆ Faster Parallel Batch-Dynamic Algorithms for Low Out-Degree Orientation
Guy Blelloch, Andrew Brady, Laxman Dhulipala, Jeremy Fineman, Kishen Gowda, Chase Hutton
A low out-degree orientation directs each edge of an undirected graph with the goal of minimizing the maximum out-degree of a vertex. In the parallel batch-dynamic setting, one can insert or delete batches of edges, and the goal is to process the entire batch in parallel with work per edge similar to that of a single sequential update and with span (or depth) for the entire batch that is polylogarithmic. In this paper we present work-efficient parallel batch-dynamic algorithms for maintaining a low out-degree orientation of an undirected graph, both in the amortized and worst-case settings. All results herein achieve polylogarithmic depth; the focus of this paper is on minimizing the work, which varies across results. In the amortized setting, we give a parallel batch-dynamic algorithm that maintains a $O(c)$-orientation in $O(\log n)$ work per update in expectation, where $c$ is a known upper bound on the arboricity over the update sequence. Our algorithm has optimal work in expectation. This result is the parallelization of the classic dynamic orientation algorithm of Brodal and Fagerberg [WADS '99], and, in this setting, is a logarithmic factor faster than the best prior parallel amortized algorithm of Liu et al. [SPAA '22]. In the worst-case setting, we give an $O(c+\log n)$-orientation with worst-case expected work per update $O(\log n)$. This is work-efficient, matching the best known sequential dynamic work of Berglin and Brodal [Algorithmica '20], and implies the existence of an $O(c)$-orientation algorithm with $O(\log^2 n)$ worst-case expected work per update. Both of our algorithms also have deterministic bounds with an additional logarithmic factor in the work. Similar to Berglin and Brodal, by adjusting the parameters of our worst-case algorithm, we achieve tradeoffs where the work is faster than $O(\log n)$ in expectation per update but the max out-degree is worse.

Recent GPU generations include special-purpose ray tracing (RT) cores for graphics applications. While RT cores are primarily used for rendering, recent works show they can be leveraged for general-purpose tasks, including similarity searches. However, existing approaches do not support datasets exceeding three dimensions. In this work, we propose RT-HiSS, the first exact GPU RT-core-based similarity search algorithm for high-dimensional datasets. GPU similarity search often scales poorly for large datasets with substantial search distances. To address this, RT-HiSS uses RT cores for fast index construction and searches, followed by candidate refinement on CUDA cores. We introduce a two-pass approach to estimate an upper bound on result size, enabling efficient batching under GPU memory constraints with near-perfect load balancing. Additionally, we examine shared memory tiling and compressed result masks to improve GPU resource utilization. RT-HiSS yields speedups up to 8.37$\times$ over competitive state-of-the-art GPU algorithms across six real-world datasets.

Generative AI (GenAI) has transformed applications in natural language processing and content creation, yet centralized inference remains hindered by high latency, limited customizability, and privacy concerns. Deploying large models (LMs) in mobile edge networks emerges as a promising solution. However, it also poses new challenges, including heterogeneous multi-modal LMs with diverse resource demands and inference speeds, varied prompt/output modalities that complicate orchestration, and resource-limited infrastructure ill-suited for concurrent LM execution. In response, we propose a Multi-Agentic AI framework for latency- and fairness-aware multi-modal LM inference in mobile edge networks. Our solution includes a long-term Global Planning Agent, a short-term Prompt Scheduling Agent, and multiple on-node LM Deployment Agents, all powered by foundation language models. These agents cooperatively optimize prompt routing and LM deployment through natural language reasoning over runtime telemetry and historical experience. To evaluate its performance, we further develop a city-wide testbed that supports network monitoring, containerized LM deployment, intra-server resource management, and inter-server communications. Experiments demonstrate that our solution reduces average end-to-end latency by 42.9% compared with a state-of-the-art online-learning baseline and by 80.6% compared with the full-activation baseline, while maintaining a mean service-type Jain's index of 0.925. Moreover, our solution adapts quickly without fine-tuning, offering a generalizable solution for optimizing GenAI services in edge environments.

This paper introduces Nemo-Nemo, a practical crash-fault tolerant (CFT) consensus protocol designed to outperform existing protocols in wide-area networks by bridging design principles from the CFT and Byzantine-fault tolerant (BFT) worlds. By structuring command propagation through a causally ordered DAG, Nemo-Nemo allows all consensus replicas to propose commands with a naturally self-regulating communication regime. By exploiting multi-leader architecture, Nemo-Nemo avoids the performance bottleneck inherent to single-leader protocols. By separating command dissemination from consensus logic, Nemo-Nemo handles challenging network conditions even when consensus commits are stalled. Moreover, leader proposals that miss a deadline are never dropped, but deterministically deferred and executed later, preserving throughput under transient network delays. And by enabling Nemo-Nemo to commit on a DAG in just two network hops, it matches the latency of existing CFT systems, while achieving significantly higher throughput. The result is a robust, deployable system: the first DAG-based CFT consensus protocol proven to exceed state-of-the-art wide-area network performance in both speed and resilience.

Nicklas Nidhögg
A certified split point lets a parallel lexer cut unlexed input at a single byte with the serial token stream provably preserved, but several conventional token sets in the predecessor's controlled study certify no byte once string, comment, or whitespace-run forms are included (arXiv:2608.03473v2). We generalize from a byte to a bounded window, a byte string after which the position where the current token began is known, regardless of surrounding context. We certify the directly usable form of that recovery, namely that the token covering the window's final byte begins at the reported origin. The certificate is conditional on occurrence and may be vacuous; every applicability figure counts only windows carrying an asserted completely tokenizable occurrence witness. We give a conservative model of a maximal-munch scanner's possible histories across a window, prove it sound, and decide reachability in that model exactly by exhausting a finite quotient of its reachable configurations. Within the flat, completely tokenizable scope, model-positive answers are semantic certificates; negatives are relative to the model, which deliberately refuses some windows a greedy scanner would allow. Whether the model certifies any window, plain or witnessed, is PSPACE-complete, and a shortest window can need $2^{Ω(\sqrt{n})}$ bytes over n live states. Two smaller searches decide plain model existence, the second shipped in release 2.2.0 of munch. In a sample of 400 random token sets, 322 of the 337 sets certifying no byte gain a witnessed window, with zero inconclusive searches, and every exact-empty row of the predecessor's study gains a witnessed window of two to four bytes. The analysis runs once after automaton construction, using only the compiled tables and no input. A boundary profile marks each gap of a window forced, crossed or open, and a window-local cut is sound exactly at forced gaps.

♻ ☆ Certified Split Points for Parallel Lexing: Exact and Modulo Discarded Tokens SP
Nicklas Nidhögg
Table-driven DFA lexing is sequential, since each transition depends on the previous byte's state. Scanning one input in parallel needs each chunk's entry state, which existing methods recover by simulation, speculation, prescanning, or overlap. We give two conditions under which none is needed. For a longest-match scanner restarting from q0 at every token boundary, a byte b is a certified split symbol when no reachable state other than q0 has a b-transition whose target can reach acceptance, and q0 is not re-entrant if it has one. Every occurrence of such a byte in completely tokenizable input begins a token, so chunks starting there reproduce the serial sequence of kinds and lengths. The condition is necessary and sufficient, but one string, comment, or whitespace run can remove every useful certificate. Comments and whitespace are usually discarded, so we weaken the guarantee to equality after deleting a declared discarded set and give a second condition, a precomputed constant-time one-bit test. It is sound but incomplete and more permissive, strictly so on suitable token sets and discarded sets. It recovers newline for a conventional C-like tokenization and tab, newline and carriage return for JSON, and refuses newline where block comments are unrestricted. Safety modulo the discarded set is decidable in PSPACE for every token automaton and in polynomial time for literal vocabularies, and every unsafe byte has a replayable counterexample. On the fifteen token sets studied the second condition is already exact. Splitting at exact certificates in munch reaches 92.6-95.3% parallel efficiency at eight threads on a restricted CPU set and a 512 MiB corpus, and a 3.46-3.94x end-to-end speedup at four threads, on one machine. It turns delimiter-based parallel lexing from a language-specific assumption into a property a compiler checks.

☆ ZipFusion: Fusing Lossless KV Decompression with Attention for Efficient LLM Decoding
Yuetao Chen, Peng Wang, Hong Xu
The key-value (KV) cache places growing demands on GPU memory capacity and bandwidth as large language models serve longer contexts and more concurrent requests. Its footprint limits concurrency, while repeated KV reads during attention can make decoding memory-bandwidth bound. Prior lossless KV cache compression methods reduce transfers between devices but restore the uncompressed KV cache in GPU memory before attention. They therefore leave these repeated KV reads unchanged and require additional work and memory for decompression. We present ZipFusion, which enables attention to consume the losslessly compressed KV cache directly. ZipFusion co-designs the compression format and attention kernel to reduce the bytes read from GPU memory during attention. The kernel reconstructs the original values directly in registers using simple bit operations, avoiding a separate decompression pass and easing the memory-bandwidth bound. ZipFusion also reassigns memory freed by compression across layers to store additional KV cache. Its memory manager reserves space for ongoing generation and makes the remaining capacity available to new requests. We implement ZipFusion on top of FlashInfer and integrate it with SGLang. On an NVIDIA H100, ZipFusion achieves about 1.25x speedup over FlashInfer in decode attention. With 8K context, it improves model decode throughput by up to 26.3% over uncompressed SGLang under the same GPU memory budget. At each method's largest supported batch, it also delivers up to 2.76x the throughput of the best-performing lossless KV cache compression baseline.

On the open Web, retrieved pages can steer the assessors that read them, and assessors from one model family fail together. On five public benchmarks with two of seven assessors adversarial, Astral lowers pooled attack success to 21.5-53.1%, against 54.7-77.8% for majority voting. The cost is coverage, as without attack 16.0-61.7% of claims receive a binary verdict and the rest are disputed for audit. Our code runs at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Astral-55F1.

Furthermore, our study reveals that overall system performance depends not only on HA speed, but also on O/S overheads, resource availability, and scheduling decisions. ♻ ☆ Retrofitting Service Dependency Discovery in Distributed Systems
Diogo Landau, Gijs Blanken, Jorge Barbosa, Nishant Saurabh
Modern distributed systems rely on complex networks of interconnected services, creating direct or indirect dependencies that can propagate faults and cause cascading failures. To localize the root cause of performance degradation in these environments, constructing a service dependency graph is highly beneficial. However, building an accurate service dependency graph is impaired by complex routing techniques, such as Network Address Translation (NAT), an essential mechanism for connecting services across networks. NAT obfuscates the actual hosts running the services, causing existing run-time approaches that passively observe network metadata to fail in accurately inferring service dependencies. To this end, this paper introduces Ripple, a run-time system for constructing process-level service dependency graphs. It operates without source code instrumentation and remains resilient under complex network routing mechanisms, including NAT. Ripple implements a non-disruptive method of injecting metadata onto a TCP packet's header that maintains protocol correctness across host boundaries. In other words, if no receiving agent is present, the instrumentation leaves existing TCP connections unaffected, ensuring non-disruptive operation when it is partially deployed across hosts. We evaluated Ripple extensively against three state-of-the-art systems across nine scenarios, involving three network configurations (NAT-free, internal-NAT, external-NAT) and three microservice benchmarks. Ripple was the only approach that performed consistently across networking configurations. With regards to correctness, it performed on par with, or better than, the state-of-the-art with precision and recall values of 100% in the majority of the scenarios.

☆ A Deterministic Security Runtime for LLM Agents on MPI and Batch-Scheduled HPC Systems: Consensus-Governed, Hardware-Rooted Supervision of Every Rank

Large language model agents launch simulations on high-performance computing (HPC) systems, where one sbatch or mpirun can commit thousands of node-hours and a forged result can cost lives. Of 23 surveyed systems, none supervises the running job, and none holds when the control host is compromised. We fix both. Enclawed, our deterministic security runtime for AI agents, has until now served a single user; this work makes it a distributed runtime for parallel HPC and agent swarms. The Enclaweder, our hardware root of trust, keeps a compromised host from becoming a catastrophe. A launch gate decides every launch by policy alone, refusing what it cannot parse. Once the job runs, a swarm chain grants short leases against signed heartbeats and evicts on evidence, and a supervisor around every rank pauses it when its lease lapses and kills it on tampering. Each node signs with its Enclaweder's key, so the host can forge none of it. Enclawed needs no administrator privileges and plugs into existing clusters unchanged, over Secure Shell alone. Supervision leaves the compute loop of a 16-rank LAMMPS job unchanged, on graphics processors too, and adds about 3 s of start-up. Twelve live attacks on Enclaweder-keyed ranks, colluding coordinators included, ended fail-closed. Sixteen agents on a real model attempted 24 launches that planted instructions ordered; the gate denied all 24 and allowed all 108 legitimate ones. Enclawed's core and the HPC Agent Security Benchmark are open source.

Computational notebooks reserve a GPU for the whole session, yet the GPU computes only while a cell executes and sits idle otherwise. Serverless execution would release the GPU between cells, but reconstructing the accumulated notebook state on a fresh worker imposes substantial cost on every GPU cell. This paper presents LooseLeaf, a serverless GPU platform for interactive notebooks. LooseLeaf derives the state and import closures of each cell, the minimal variables and packages that the cell needs. Our analysis on 5,000 real-world notebooks shows that these closures are small, and user-cell editing leaves seconds to prepare them. LooseLeaf prepares a GPU worker with these closures while the user edits the cell. After execution, the worker saves the updated state within seconds, so the GPU is reclaimable after every cell. LooseLeaf starts 95-98% of GPU cells with no visible delay, matches the interactivity of a pinned session, and provisions 32-55% fewer GPU-hours than state-of-the-art notebook platforms.

To bridge this gap, we develop a native EnergyPlus object, ElectricEquipment:ITE:LiquidCooled, that models DTC liquid cooling for chilled-water and warm-water architectures as plant-loop components. It couples facility-water loops, rack-side secondary loops, coolant distribution units, and chip-junction temperatures within a single solver. Validation against an independent Modelica implementation across 21 operating conditions, including two full-year runs compared at one-minute resolution, yields loop-temperature RMSE at or below 0.021 K, well within the 0.1 K acceptance threshold. By embedding liquid-cooling logic into EnergyPlus, our work provides whole-building, long-term energy modeling for high-density AI infrastructure within an open-source framework.

☆ On Latency-Optimal Implementations of the Timestamp Object
Aurojit Panda, Scott Shenker, Sam Toueg, Wen Zhang
Timestamps are widely used in distributed algorithms to order operations. In this paper, we study the timestamp object (TS), which provides a single operation that returns strictly increasing integers. We ask two questions: What is the maximum resilience and the minimum latency of TS implementations in asynchronous message-passing systems, where latency is measured by worst-case message delay? We answer these questions under various types of failure: crash failures, and Byzantine failures with and without digital signatures. To do so, we give lower bounds and algorithms that determine (1) the optimal resilience of TS implementations under each type of failure, and (2) the optimal latency in all cases but one. Along the way, we introduce a new lower-bound proof technique called a cyclic chain argument, which constructs a cycle of indistinguishable schedules along which the returned timestamps must strictly increase, yielding a contradiction.
☆ Quantum Cadence: Post-Quantum Consensus with Multiple Concurrent Proposers
Mohammad Mussadiq Jalalzai, Tobias Klenze, Jovan Komatovic
The consensus protocols of most high-performance blockchains use quorum certificates, which bundle the signatures of a quorum of validators. Signature schemes such as BLS can aggregate the signatures of a whole quorum into a single short signature, which keeps these certificates small. A large-scale quantum computer would break these schemes, and no post-quantum scheme with comparable aggregate size and aggregation time is known. Without aggregation, a certificate holds one large post-quantum signature per member of the quorum, so it becomes infeasible for each validator to broadcast certificates, as modern consensus protocols often require. We present Quantum Cadence, a post-quantum consensus protocol with multiple concurrent proposers that avoids certificates altogether: every validator counts quorums among the messages it has received itself. Its safety and liveness do not even depend on signatures, although we add signatures to obtain accountability. Quantum Cadence builds on Cadence and replaces its slot consensus, Chorus, with Quantum Chorus, which keeps the optimal fast-path latency of Chorus: dissemination followed by two rounds of votes. When its fast path fails, Quantum Chorus runs Coda, our signature-free Byzantine agreement for multiple proposers. We also outline how the Conductor, which schedules the slots of Cadence, can be adapted to Quantum Cadence. In simulations with 200 validators, Quantum Chorus has a latency comparable to that of Chorus and scales better with the number of proposers.

☆ Clean-label Poisoning Attack and Defense Game for Federated Learning in Vehicular Networks
Yalin E. Sagduyu, Tugba Erpek, Nathan Stephenson, Mengran Xue
This paper studies interactions between clean-label poisoning attack and defense in vehicular networks using federated learning (FL). Basic Safety Message (BSM) classification for anomaly detection is modeled as a distributed learning problem over a vehicular network with dynamic topology. As a critical threat to FL, a feature-space clean-label attack is introduced, wherein benign samples are perturbed toward malicious feature extremes, degrading class separability while preserving labels. To counter this, a feature-consistency relabeling defense is proposed to detect and relabel suspicious samples. A game-theoretic framework is developed to capture attack-defense interactions and characterize equilibrium strategies based on attack effectiveness and cost parameters. Results show that the attack scales effectively with compromised nodes, while the proposed defense keeps attack success low without degrading clean accuracy and shifts equilibrium regions toward attack-averse regimes.
☆ Migration as a Steady-State Execution Primitive: A Runtime for Virtual Stationarity in Low-Earth Orbit
Daniel Kleebinder, Alireza Furutanpey, Stefan Nastic
Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite mega-constellations enable orbital edge computing for latency-critical geocentric applications, but satellite motion compresses line-of-sight communication windows to mere minutes. To maintain logical geographic proximity, a paradigm termed Virtual Stationarity (VS), applications must continuously migrate across passing satellites in the constellation. Traditional live migration mechanisms optimize individually initiated relocations or replication, but not the continuous handover between successive hosts that orbital motion requires. We reformulate live migration as a steady-state execution model and introduce a novel virtual stationarity runtime paradigm. We formalize the viability of continuous migration through a lightweight model capturing latency and availability service-level objectives (SLOs), continuous migration overhead, and the convergence bound of state replay. To satisfy these constraints, we derive a Virtual Stationarity Runtime (VSR) framework whose Migration Membrane combines Capability Virtualization and Continuous State Projection to rebind host resources and reconstruct evolving execution on a successor. Evaluation on physical heterogeneous hosts shows 95th-percentile downtime below 6 milliseconds across 300 recurrent handovers, migration time effectively invariant to memory-write rate, and no cumulative growth in migration time or continuation state. A 1,600-satellite simulation further confirms completion within orbital handover windows.

☆ Beyond Hotness: High-Resolution Memory Characterization of Cloud and LLM Workloads for Tiered Memory with ARM SPE

Memory demands from data analytics and LLM workloads grow rapidly, driving up memory costs in cloud and data centers. Multi-tier memory has emerged as a promising solution to balance performance and cost. However, effectively leveraging it requires a deep understanding of workload memory behaviors. This work introduces a high-resolution memory characterization methodology for analyzing workload-specific opportunities for multi-tier memory usage. In response to the increasing deployment of ARM-based processors in data centers, we implement our methodology using the recent Statistical Profiling Extension (SPE) for ARM. By characterizing eight memory-intensive workloads from CloudSuite and LLM applications, we identify region-specific access patterns, evaluate the effectiveness of cloud-oriented cache hierarchies, and propose new metrics based on memory idle periods and latency profiles to determine suitable data placement for tiered memory.
☆ Tile-Based Decompression in Compiled GPU Engines VLDB
Antonio Boffa, Ananya Gupta, Hamish Nicholson, Anastasia Ailamaki
Modern GPUs reach record analytical performance only when a query's working set fits within its GPU memory budget, and that budget is under growing pressure: GPUs are partitioned and shared, working sets are outgrowing high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and HBM is a fixed on-device resource whose per-dollar capacity has stagnated across generations. Lightweight compression can relieve this pressure by shrinking both footprint and bandwidth demand, but existing GPU compressed-execution techniques either bind decompression to a specific execution model or materialize decompressed columns in HBM before query execution. We present a compression subsystem for compiled GPU query engines that treats decompression as a first-class physical operator. Compression-specific logic is isolated behind a narrow backend interface, so new GPU-oriented encodings can be added without rewriting downstream operators. We implement the design in Proteus and study where decompressed values should be materialized in the GPU memory hierarchy. Our compiler-integrated shared-memory strategy fuses cooperative tile decompression with tuple-at-a-time query execution inside a single generated GPU kernel, avoiding decompressed-column materialization in HBM. Compared with HeavyDB and Sirius on GPU-resident data, fused on-chip decompression achieves competitive query times while reducing the resident memory footprint by up to 4x and memory-bandwidth consumption by up to 6x.

☆ InferSlice: A Reference Architecture for SLO-driven LLM Inference over a Telco Wide-Area Network
Juan Parra-Ullauri, Anthony Chiu, Hari Madhukumar, Zhaozhou Wu, Anderson Bravalheri, Alex Healing, Andy Corston-Petrie, Dimitra Simeonidou, Nektaria Efthymiou
LLM inference is increasingly deployed as a core service for enterprise and interactive applications, but sovereignty, compliance, latency and resource-locality requirements can limit the suitability of centralised cloud deployments. Telco operators offer geographically distributed compute and network infrastructure for addressing these constraints. However, existing LLM serving frameworks are designed for tightly coupled data centres and provide limited support for coordinating geographically distributed and heterogeneous resources. We present InferSlice, a reference architecture for Service-Level Objective (SLO)-driven LLM inference over a telco infrastructure, integrating network slicing, GPU partitioning, elastic serving and observability. Led by BT in collaboration with the University of Bristol and NVIDIA, and realised on the JOINER UK national-scale wide-area network (WAN), InferSlice is evaluated on service differentiation across tiers, elastic scale-out, client-edge bandwidth as a bottleneck, and the reach of tensor, pipeline, data parallelism, and prefill/decode disaggregation over the WAN. Our results show that, on a general-purpose telco network, tiers yield distinct latency-throughput regimes, and weight streaming shortens scale-out time. Replication is placement-insensitive but memory-bound; pipeline parallelism tolerates near- and mid-cross-site hops, while tensor parallelism and disaggregation fail beyond a single subnet hop. We share practical insights from operating SLO-driven inference on a telco network, lessons learned and open questions, and hope to encourage further research on distributed and heterogeneous LLM inference systems.
☆ GLP Networking API Specification
Dan Bachar, Ehud Shapiro
Multiagent deterministic GLP (madGLP) runs Grassroots Logic Programs (GLP) as agents that communicate solely by asynchronous message passing, and assumes fair delivery: every message sent is eventually delivered. Each agent runs on a person's smartphone, named by the person's public key. A grassroots platform depends on no global resource but the network, so agents must reach one another over Bluetooth Low Energy, on a local network, and across the Internet from behind NAT, via rendezvous servers anyone can run. What madGLP requires of such a network, and what the network requires of the platform, has not been specified. We specify the networking layer beneath madGLP. Anything that can be done in GLP is done in GLP: the layer provides only what GLP cannot reach - the network stack, the location service, application attestation, and cryptographic primitives. Three transport underlays share one interface. Over PAN and LAN, an agent advertises a rotating recognition token derived from its key and time slot, so a peer who knows the key recognises it before contact and nobody else can track it; whether it answers unrecognised contacts is a per-underlay trust level set by GLP. Over WAN, a rendezvous server is a static-address host running the headless layer and a GLP rendezvous agent that coordinates hole punching, relays no payload, and belongs to no social graph. On every underlay, peers establish a mutually authenticated Noise session from Ed25519 keys, then attest, bound to the handshake hash, that each runs the application published under its developer's key, verified against Apple's and Google's roots with no third party contacted. One message protocol, over UDP datagrams and GATT writes, provides the fair, unordered, atomic and authenticated delivery madGLP assumes.
☆ On the Expressiveness of Asynchronous Processes with Nested Session Types
Sjors Wortelboer, Dan Frumin, Jorge A. Pérez
Session types are a type-based approach to correct message-passing programs, where types specify protocols for channels and type checking guarantees communication correctness. Traditional session types express regular protocols only, which leaves out many protocols found in practice. Aiming at overcoming this limitation, Nested Session Types (NSTs) can specify nested recursive protocols. NSTs are known to be characterised by one-counter machines and deterministic context-free languages. In this paper, we study the expressiveness of ASP (Asynchronous Session Processes), the process model associated with NSTs as introduced by Das et al. We prove that AST is Turing complete by giving a correct encoding of two-counter machines into typed processes. Our encoding uses a non-trivial state-aware representation of counters and instructions that is neatly governed by NSTs.

☆ Data Quality Audit and Bivariate Temperature-Humidity Analysis of a Long-Term LoRaWAN Network: Anomaly Detection, PCA, Clustering and Machine Learning
Mamadou Sow
Long-term environmental IoT/LPWAN deployments often aggregate heterogeneous data streams from diverse devices without systematic auditing of each variable's actual coverage prior to analysis-an increased risk when multiple sensor types coexist within the same network. This work proposes a C++17 processing pipeline applied to the Tour Perret LoRaWAN dataset (421 937 frames, June 2021--June 2023, 5 devices). A systematic coverage audit integrated into the extraction phase reveals that CO2 is completely missing (0% coverage) and pressure is reported only by an isolated base module (Wyres, 4.24% of the corpus), invalidating the initial hypothesis of a joint four-variable analysis. The analysis is refocused on the Temperature--Humidity pair, jointly available across 205{,}005 frames (95.76%) from 4 Elsys EMS sensors. The pipeline sequentially performs anomaly detection (modified Z-score, Isolation Forest), bivariate Principal Component Analysis, clustering (K-means, DBSCAN), and a multilayer perceptron predicting humidity from temperature and time, whose residuals serve as a detector for slow drift. On real-world data: Temperature--Humidity correlation r=-0.662, two-component PCA (PC1 =83.1% of variance), Isolation Forest detects 2.12% multivariate anomalies while univariate Z-score detects none, calibrated DBSCAN isolates 0.17% noise across 13 clusters, and the MLP achieves $R^2=0.672$ (RMSE =10.54%) in cross-validation. This work demonstrates that per-variable coverage auditing prior to modeling is a necessary methodological step for heterogeneous multi-sensor IoT datasets.
☆ KnitTrans: Coordinated Trajectory Transfer for Effective and Efficient LLM Reinforcement Learning
Bangjun Xiao, Chiheng Lou, Xiaodong Ji, Xiangwei Deng, Yikai Zhao, Gang Huang, Hailin Zhang
Trajectory transfer from rollout to training affects both learning quality and system efficiency in large language model reinforcement learning (RL). Enforcing batch-wide training requirements can delay the admission of completed trajectories, resulting in higher architectural staleness: the additional parameter-version gap from disaggregated pipelining relative to colocated execution. Beyond admission, misalignment between data access and training consumption causes redundant movement and unnecessary waiting when transferring large trajectory payloads. We present KnitTrans, a system that coordinates the rollout-to-training path through three designs. First, constraint-preserving mini-batch admission allows flexibility in early mini-batch composition, while checking that enough capacity remains to satisfy the remaining quotas. Second, on-demand trajectory data access matches storage units to consumer assignments and overlaps micro-batch data preparation with computation. Third, multimodal encoding deduplication supports reuse across a mini-batch while preserving gradient contributions from all backbone micro-batches. Experiments show up to 93% lower architectural staleness than with train-batch admission, narrowing the learning-quality gap between disaggregated execution and colocated execution. On multimodal workloads, KnitTrans reduces transfer latency by two orders of magnitude and achieves a speedup of up to 5.8 times in transfer plus training over the baseline.

Zebin Ren, Biao Cao, Kang Chen, Zhihui Yin, Qiushi Chen, Jielong Jian, Jiwei Xiong, Xinxing Wang, Yan Xing, Liguo Duan, Ran Zheng, Xianjun Meng, Zhenyu Hou
Storage systems in production increasingly rely on distributed databases for metadata management, yet our experience at Baidu shows that treating a general-purpose database as a black box leaves substantial performance and efficiency untapped. File-system metadata exhibits directory-tree locality, differentiated consistency requirements, and clustered deletions that general-purpose databases largely ignore. We thus propose MetaDB, a metadata-aware distributed transactional database that serves as the shared metadata layer for Baidu's large-scale storage systems. MetaDB addresses three key mismatches between general-purpose databases and metadata workloads: Data Model Mismatch, Transaction Model Mismatch, and Storage Implementation Mismatch. To bridge these gaps, MetaDB combines (1) tree-topology-induced sharding and execution, (2) semantic-aware off-critical-path processing, and (3) a lifecycle-aware storage engine with in-memory MVCC and locality-aware compaction. MetaDB achieves 2.2x-4.1x the throughput of our previous general-purpose database and halves the number of metadata machines. Deployed in production at Baidu for over five years, MetaDB unifies metadata management across the company's storage fleet and scales to over 1,000 metadata nodes, tens of trillions of metadata records, and exabyte-scale storage in a single cluster.

♻ ☆ Merge Hulls Without Copying Vertices: GPU Isotonic Regression
Elena Raikova
Isotonic regression finds the monotone sequence closest to the data in weighted least squares. It is used to calibrate probabilities and inside differentiable ranking. Its standard algorithm, pool adjacent violators, is sequential within a sequence, and torchsort, the exact GPU solver of differentiable sorting libraries, runs it with one thread per sequence, which is slow on long ones. The fit is the slope sequence of the lower convex hull of cumulative sums, and hulls of sorted points can be merged in parallel. Merging partial hulls level by level, however, copies the surviving vertices at every level, which moves Theta(n log n) data when most points survive. We store each chunk's hull once and represent a merged hull as a list of segments of these chunk hulls, at most one per chunk; a merge then updates the list. We prove the representation correct, bound the work and depth of the merge phase, and measure a CUDA implementation on four NVIDIA GPUs against a control that copies the surviving vertices with the whole GPU at every level. On dense hulls the merge phase is 17 to 276 times faster with segment lists and the whole operator 3.9 to 19 times; on noisy data, where few vertices survive, the difference is small. In a differentiable soft rank, replacing torchsort's isotonic solver makes forward and backward 1.8 to 820 times faster, and the training step of a compact model with a Spearman loss 1.5 to 40 times. Code: https://github.com/LenaBarretta/torchisotonic

♻ ☆ A Real-time tax compliance architecture for VAT split payments with Making Tax Smart and Open Banking
Panos Louvieris, George Ioannou, Gareth White
This paper presents Making Tax Smart with Open Banking (MTS-OB), a novel DLT-based architecture designed to integrate real-time VAT compliance into the existing payment system through split payments and Open Banking. Motivated by the substantial VAT gap, the research investigates how leveraging the informational value embedded within payment transactions can reduce the tax administration burden. MTS-OB, a proof-of-concept application built on R3 Corda, facilitates automated, real-time VAT split payments (VSP) without disrupting current payment infrastructure. MTS-OB integrates with existing banking systems via Open Banking APIs, enabling secure information management for VAT collection, reporting, analytics, and automated compliance enforcement. The system uses traditional bank deposit money as a real-time information sensor thereby extending its functionality to include "money as a medium of real-time taxation". Scalability testing demonstrates the system's ability to maintain operational stability under increasing transaction loads, illustrating its potential for real-world deployment. The key finding is the necessity of redefining money to include its informational value for real-time tax compliance, requiring a redesign of the money system while adhering to existing regulations and standards. This research demonstrates the feasibility of integrating tax functionality directly into payments, offering a path towards "hard to get tax wrong" compliance and a potential reduction in the VAT gap without compromising financial stability.
♻ ☆ Power- and Fragmentation-aware Online Scheduling for GPU Datacenters
Francesco Lettich, Emanuele Carlini, Franco Maria Nardini, Raffaele Perego, Salvatore Trani
The rise of Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models is driving increased GPU usage in data centers for complex training and inference tasks, impacting operational costs, energy demands, and the environmental footprint of large-scale computing infrastructures. This work addresses the online scheduling problem in GPU datacenters, which involves scheduling tasks without knowledge of their future arrivals. We focus on two objectives: minimizing GPU fragmentation and reducing power consumption. GPU fragmentation occurs when partial GPU allocations hinder the efficient use of remaining resources, especially as the datacenter nears full capacity. A recent scheduling policy, Fragmentation Gradient Descent (FGD), leverages a fragmentation metric to address this issue. Reducing power consumption is also crucial due to the significant power demands of GPUs. To this end, we propose PWR, a novel scheduling policy to minimize power usage by selecting power-efficient GPU and CPU combinations. This involves a simplified model for measuring power consumption integrated into a Kubernetes score plugin. Through an extensive experimental evaluation in a simulated cluster, we show how PWR, when combined with FGD, achieves a balanced trade-off between reducing power consumption and minimizing GPU fragmentation.

We present the design of a Resource-Aware Task Allocator (RATA) and an empirical analysis in handling real-time tasks for processing on Distributed Satellite Systems (DSS). We consider task processing performance across low Earth orbit (LEO) to Low-Medium Earth Orbit (Low-MEO) constellation sizes, under varying traffic loads. Using Single-Level Tree Network(SLTN)-based cooperative task allocation architecture, we attempt to evaluate some key performance metrics - blocking probabilities, response times, energy consumption, and resource utilization across several tens of thousands of tasks per experiment. Our resource-conscious RATA monitors key parameters such as arrival rate, resources (on-board compute, storage, bandwidth, battery) availability, satellite eclipses' influence in processing and communications. This study is an important step towards analyzing the performance under lighter to stress inducing levels of compute intense workloads to test the ultimate performance limits under the combined influence of the above-mentioned factors. Results show pronounced non-linear scaling: while capacity increases with constellation size, blocking and delay grow rapidly, whereas energy remains resilient under solar-aware scheduling. The analysis identifies a practical satellite-count limit for baseline SLTNs and demonstrates that CPU availability, rather than energy, is the primary cause of blocking. These findings provide quantitative guidance by identifying thresholds at which system performance shifts from graceful degradation to collapse.
♻ ☆ From a Last-Week Add-On to First-Day Practice: Three Years of Integrating MPI Performance Analysis into HPC Education with EduMPI Suite SC26
Anna-Lena Roth, Jonas Posner
Performance analysis is essential for scalable MPI programs, yet tool and workflow complexity often relegates it to the end of Parallel Programming courses. EduMPI Suite lowers this entry barrier by automating cluster execution, measurement, and near-real-time analysis while visualizing MPI communication from the first program. This paper presents a three-year experience report on its integration into HPC education. We trace the transition of performance analysis from a last-week add-on to a recurring element of MPI development, using unpublished historical survey evidence and individual 2025 questionnaire data. Earlier cohorts perceived performance analysis as unnecessary, difficult, or unintuitive. In the final study, all students recommended introducing EduMPI Suite early in the course. Of 33 students, 29-33 rated it higher than conventional tools for understanding program behavior, interpreting communication, identifying bottlenecks, obtaining visual feedback, and navigating the tool. These findings support embedding performance analysis throughout MPI education before transitioning learners to professional environments.

♻ ☆ HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
Junhyeok Park, Jungeun Yoon, Kyungmin Kim, Hunsoon Lee, Shinyoung Ahn, Kangho Kim
Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts. To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed directly without additional data rearrangement while maintaining transfer efficiency. We implement and evaluate HAWK on a system built with commercially available GPUs and NPUs, demonstrating performance within 7.88% of a GPU-only system under the same SLO constraints while achieving up to 1.26$\times$ higher power efficiency and 1.72$\times$ higher cost efficiency.
